title: Fake Leadership? 8 Signs You're Performing Leadership, Not Practicing It
author: The Good Boss
summary: Opening with an anecdote about a senior leader at a career fair who could not say what he actually did, the author argues that a leader's job splits into identity and work, and that many people do the first while calling it the second. He lists eight signs of performed leadership, including titles that take longer to say than the job, borrowed seniority, buzzword-heavy roles, meetings that settle nothing, a growing coordination layer, exhaustion without output, busyness as proof, and silent best people. He admits to committing several of these himself, which gives the diagnosis credibility. His underlying claim is that vague language and busyness are ways to hide from the risk of deciding. He ends with the observation that AI has removed the expensive props, leaving judgment, courage, clarity and ownership as the real work.
points: Real leadership is described as seeing the problem, making a decision and owning the outcome, and buzzwords exist to avoid that risk.
A title confers permission but not power, which is built by making decisions and living with the results.
Meetings that repeatedly end with take-it-offline signal fear of being wrong, not collaboration.
A coordination layer growing faster than output means complexity is being manufactured rather than managed.
When the best people stop pushing back it may mean they have given up on the leader, not that they are engaged.
quotes: I’ve spent 20+ years in tech leadership, and I have observed that the leader’s job has been split into two parts: the identity and the work. Most people are doing the first one and calling it the second.

A title gives you the permission, but doesn’t necessarily give you the power. Permission lets you speak in the meeting, but real power is something you build by making decisions and living with the outcome of those decisions.
In my experience, real leadership is actually much simpler: You see the problem, make a decision, and own the outcome. That’s all.
The real issue was fear - nobody wanted to make the call and risk being “wrong”, so the team “performed collaboration” instead of making a decision.
If your coordination layer is growing faster than your output, you’re not managing complexity. You’re manufacturing it.

Leaders who “perform” confidence usually think they’re building trust, but they’re doing quite the opposite. The moment your team senses you’re performing instead of deciding, they lose trust in you, and eventually, respect in you.
What is left today is the part AI can’t do: judgment, courage, clarity, and owning the outcome when it goes wrong.
